The roadmap What matters now Ireland The UK Oxford Money & scholarships For grown-ups

Maya, here is the road to becoming a doctor

You are in 4th class now. Becoming a doctor takes a long time, but the road is clear, and every step on it is one you can take. This page maps the whole journey, in Ireland and in the UK, including Oxford, and answers the money questions too.

Now: 4th class, age 9 Medical school: 5 or 6 years Fully trained GP: about 10 years after starting Two doors: Ireland, or the UK and Oxford

One honest note before we start. Every fee, points score and exam rule on this page is how things stand for students applying in 2025 and 2026. You will not apply until about 2034 or 2035, and the numbers will have changed by then, some of them several times. The shape of the road is what lasts. The exact numbers are a photograph of today, so you can see how the system works. Research checked on 15 November 2026.

The whole journey, step by step

From 4th class to fully trained doctor. There is one big choice along the way, whether to do Transition Year, and it changes your dates. Try the switch and watch the roadmap change.

Will Maya do Transition Year? Transition Year (TY) is an optional year after 3rd year of secondary school, with no state exam. Most schools offer it, and some make it compulsory. It is a lovely year for projects and work experience, and, as you will see, it matters for Oxford.

With TY, the Oxford door opens on time. You sit the Leaving Certificate in June 2035, aged 18, and you can start at Oxford, or at any Irish medical school, that same autumn.

Without TY, there is a timing trap at Oxford. Oxford says you must be 18 by 1 November of the year you start. You would finish school in June 2034, aged 17. Irish universities would take you that September, but Oxford could not start you until October 2035, so you would need a gap year or a deferred place. Nothing is lost, but it is worth knowing now, years ahead.

  1. 9
    Now · 4th class · 2026/27

    Primary school, where you are today

    Two more years after this one: 5th class, then 6th class. There is no state exam at the end of primary school. Nothing you do at age 9 decides whether you get into medicine. What helps is what you are already doing: reading lots, enjoying science and nature, and keeping your maths strong.

  2. 12
    Ages 12 to 15 · Sept 2029 to June 2032

    Secondary school: the Junior Cycle

    Three years of lots of different subjects. At the end of 3rd year you get a Junior Cycle Profile of Achievement. Keep science and maths going, because they become very important later.

  3. TY
    Transition Year (optional)

    A year to explore

    No state exam. Work experience, projects, trips, new skills. A good year to try volunteering or shadowing in a caring job, and to find out whether looking after people is really the life you want.

  4. 16
    5th and 6th year: the Leaving Certificate years

    This is where the big subject choice happens

    At the start of 5th year you choose your Leaving Certificate subjects, and this choice really matters. The advice is simple: take Higher Level Chemistry and Higher Level Biology, with Higher Maths if you can. That pair keeps every medical school in Ireland open to you, and Chemistry is compulsory for Oxford. The full detail is in the Ireland and Oxford sections below.

  5. !
    Exam season, twice over

    Two tests decide medical school in Ireland

    In February of 6th year you sit the HPAT, a thinking test (it does not test what you learned in school). In June you sit the Leaving Certificate. Your two scores are added together, and that total decides Irish medicine places through the CAO. If Oxford or another UK school is the goal instead, the test is the UCAT, taken the summer before you apply, and the application deadline is much earlier, 15 October. Both tests are explained below.

  6. 18
    Medical school

    Five or six years of learning to be a doctor

    In Ireland the course is 5 years at some universities and 6 years at others (the 6-year ones include a foundation year). At Oxford it is 6 years. You study how the body works, then diseases and medicines, then you spend more and more time in hospitals and GP practices, learning from real doctors and real patients.

  7. +
    The year after graduating

    Intern year: your first paid job as a doctor

    In Ireland, your first year after medical school is the intern year. You are a real doctor, paid by the HSE, working in hospitals in blocks of at least 3 months of general medicine and 3 months of general surgery, plus other specialties. At the end you get a Certificate of Experience from the Medical Council. In the UK the same stage is called Foundation training, FY1 and FY2, and lasts two years.

  8. Dr
    Then you choose your kind of doctor

    GP, or hospital specialist

    To become a GP (the doctor families visit first) takes 4 more years in Ireland after the intern year: 2 years in hospital jobs, then 2 years training in a GP practice. To become a hospital consultant (a specialist, like a heart doctor or a surgeon) takes about 6 to 9 more years: 2 to 3 years of Basic Specialist Training, then 4 to 6 years of Higher Specialist Training.

    So the whole count is: about 10 years from starting medical school to fully trained GP, and roughly 12 to 15 years to consultant. On the no-TY, 5-year-degree path with no delays, that would mean graduating in 2039, finishing the intern year in 2040, qualifying as a GP around 2044, or as a consultant around 2046 to 2049. Real life often adds a year or two, because training places are competitive. That is normal, and lots of doctors take extra time along the way.

What matters now, at age 9 (and what does not)

Things that genuinely help

  • Reading, lots of it. Both big tests on this road, the HPAT and the UCAT, are really tests of understanding words, people and problems quickly.
  • Maths confidence. Doctors use numbers every day, and strong maths keeps your school options open.
  • Science curiosity. How bodies work, why we get sick, how medicines help. Ask questions, watch good science programmes, grow things, take things apart (carefully).
  • Understanding people. One whole section of the HPAT is about understanding how other people feel. Kindness is not just nice, it is literally part of the test, and most of the job.
  • Stamina and habits. Medicine is a long road. Sleeping well, finishing what you start, and not giving up on hard homework are quiet superpowers.

Things that do not matter yet

  • No exam prep. The HPAT and UCAT are nearly a decade away, they can only be taken in your final school year, and practising for them now would be pointless. The HPAT score only counts in the year you take it; it cannot be saved up.
  • No subject choices yet. The decision that matters, Chemistry and Biology at Higher Level, is made at the start of 5th year, when you are 15 or 16.
  • No need to pick Ireland or Oxford now. The same school subjects keep both doors open. The choice comes at application time, when you are 17 or 18.
  • No primary school exam. There is no state exam at the end of primary school in Ireland.

The research behind this page puts it plainly: nothing Maya does at age 9 determines entry to medicine, except building strong science and maths foundations and reading habits. The decisive choices are six or more years away.

Door one: medicine in Ireland

Ireland has six medical schools: Trinity College Dublin, UCD, RCSI, University College Cork, the University of Galway, and the University of Limerick (whose undergraduate course is new from 2026). This is the simplest and by far the cheapest route, and it works like this.

  1. Choose the right Leaving Certificate subjects. Every school needs at least 480 CAO points in one sitting, with passes in English, Irish and Maths. For the 5-year courses you need H4 in Chemistry, plus H4 in Biology or Physics (Trinity asks for H3 and H4 across two sciences). For the 6-year courses, which include a foundation year, you only need an O6/H7 pass in one science subject, and Chemistry is not compulsory. Safest plan: Higher Chemistry and Higher Biology, which keeps all six schools open.
  2. Sit the HPAT in February of 6th year. HPAT stands for Health Professions Admission Test. It is run by a company called ACER, it lasts 2½ hours, it is multiple choice, and it does not test anything you learned in school. It tests three things: logical reasoning and problem solving (40%), understanding other people (40%), and non-verbal reasoning, spotting patterns in shapes (20%). You register with ACER separately from the CAO, and the fee reported for 2027 entry was €167. Your score only counts for that one year.
  3. Apply through the CAO by 1 February of 6th year, ranking medicine alongside any other courses you like. Offers come out in August, after the Leaving Certificate results.
  4. Your two scores are added together. That combined total, not the Leaving Certificate alone, decides who gets a place. It is extremely competitive, as the chart below shows.

The score of the last student offered a place, CAO Round 1, 2025 (Limerick: its first cut-off, 2026)

Combined Leaving Certificate + HPAT score, out of 865. The bars start at 700 so you can see the small gaps between universities.

Limerick had no undergraduate entry in 2025, so its bar shows its first cut-off, from 2026. These are the scores of the last person offered a place in Round 1, not a fixed pass mark, and they move every year. In 2026 the same schools ranged from 730 to 741. Sources: CollegeRoute, Medicine CAO points; Ace the HPAT, CAO Points for Medicine 2025; UCD's own news report of its 2025 Round 1 results.

What those numbers really mean. At UCD in 2025, the student admitted with the lowest Leaving Certificate had 554 points, and they needed a very strong HPAT of at least 187 to make up the total. The student with the lowest HPAT, 173, needed at least 625 Leaving Certificate points. In plain words: you need near-top grades and a strong HPAT. Neither one on its own is enough. Source: UCD admissions, DN400 and HPAT.

Important: the scoring is changing before your turn. From 2027 entry, the system is rebalanced. Leaving Certificate points above 550 will count in full instead of being scaled down, and the HPAT will be worth a maximum of 150 instead of 300. So the biggest possible combined score becomes 775, not 865. That means the 728 to 739 figures above will not be the target in your year; the cut-offs will be published on the new scale. The 480-point minimum and the rule that the HPAT must be taken in your final year stay the same. Source: Irish Universities Association, Entry to Medicine.

What Irish medical school costs

€0
Tuition fees. Under the Free Fees Initiative, the State pays the tuition for eligible Irish and EU students at public universities, including RCSI. (Students from outside the EU pay roughly €52,000 to €61,000 a year for the same course. Maya would not pay that.)
€2,500
Maximum student contribution per year in 2026/27, reduced from €3,000 in Budget 2026. Colleges add small levies on top, so the real total is roughly €2,500 to €3,300 a year before any grant.
€4,722
Top standard SUSI maintenance grant per year (Band 1, living 30 km or more from college), plus 100% of the student contribution paid. A special rate of €7,936 exists for the lowest-income households. SUSI is means-tested on household income; Band 1 needs reckonable income under €47,010.

So in Ireland, the real cost of medical school is not tuition. It is living costs: rent, food, transport, books, and travel to hospital placements, partly covered by a SUSI grant if the family qualifies. Sources: RCSI, Medicine fees and funding; SUSI (rates via SUSI-based summaries, November 2026).

A back door, just so you know it exists

If someone does a different degree first and still wants medicine afterwards, there is graduate-entry medicine: a 4-year course that uses a different test, the GAMSAT, instead of the HPAT. It is not Maya's planned route, but it means a missed place at 18 is never the end of the story.

Door two: medicine in the UK

Maya is an Irish citizen, and that gives her a special key to the UK that almost nobody else in Europe has any more.

The Common Travel Area advantage

Because of the Common Travel Area agreement between Ireland and the UK, which survived Brexit, Irish students at UK universities pay Home fees, not international fees, and can borrow the full tuition fee from Student Finance England, as long as they have lived in Ireland, the UK or the Islands for the three years before the course starts.

At Oxford in 2026/27 that is the difference between £9,790 a year and £49,400 a year. Other EU citizens generally pay the international rate. Ireland is the exception.

The one gap: living costs

The UK loan covers tuition only. A student living in Ireland before the course is not eligible for a UK maintenance loan for living costs. GOV.UK's student finance guide for 2026/27 says so directly, and Ulster University confirms that students from the Republic of Ireland get their maintenance support from SUSI instead.

So for the UK: tuition can be borrowed and repaid later, but rent and food must come from SUSI, bursaries, family, savings or work. The money section below adds it all up.

How applying to the UK works

Maya would not need to move schools or switch to A-levels. UK medical schools accept the Irish Leaving Certificate. But the UK system runs on its own calendar, and its school stages have different names, so here is the translation:

UK stageAgesWhat happens, and Maya's equivalent
GCSEs14 to 16UK pupils take 8 to 10 subjects, including the sciences, Maths and English. Medicine applicants usually have mostly grades 7 to 9. Maya's equivalent is the Junior Cycle, and UK schools read her Leaving Certificate as her main qualification.
A-levels16 to 18Three subjects, usually Chemistry and Biology plus Physics or Maths. Typical medicine offers are AAA to A*AA. Maya applies with Leaving Certificate grades instead; Oxford's translation is in the next section.
UCAT17, the summer before applyingThe UK's admissions test, used by more than 30 medical and dental schools. About 2 hours, on a computer: Verbal Reasoning, Decision Making and Quantitative Reasoning, each scored 300 to 900 (total 300 to 2,700), plus a Situational Judgement section graded in Bands 1 to 4. Every school uses it differently; there is no single pass mark. For 2026 entry, testing ran from 7 July to 26 September 2025.
UCAS application17 to 18Deadline for medicine, and for Oxford and Cambridge, is 15 October at 18:00 UK time, much earlier than the CAO. You may choose at most 4 medicine courses out of your 5 UCAS choices; the 5th must be something else. There is a personal statement (a three-question format from 2026 entry) and a teacher reference.
Interviews17 to 18December to March. Most schools use MMIs, a circuit of short interview stations. Oxford and Cambridge interview in December, in their own style (next section).
The degree18+5 years at most UK schools; 6 years at Oxford and Cambridge, and wherever a built-in extra degree year or foundation year is included.
After graduatingTwo paid Foundation years (FY1 and FY2), rotating through specialties about every 4 months, with full GMC registration after FY1. UK graduates also pass the Medical Licensing Assessment (MLA). Then GP training takes 3 more years, or hospital specialty training 5 to 8 more years. That is about 10 years from starting medical school to GP, and about 14 to 16 years to consultant.

Sources: GOV.UK, Student finance: how you're assessed and paid, 2026 to 2027; Ulster University, student finance for Republic of Ireland students; UCAT dates and format via UCAT preparation guides summarised in the research notes.

Oxford, in detail

Oxford's medicine course has its own code, A100, and it is one of the most sought-after courses in the world. Here is exactly what it asks for, and what studying there is like.

The grades Oxford asks for

  • Leaving Certificate (Maya's route): H1 H1 H2 H2 H2 H2 at Higher Level, with Chemistry compulsory, plus at least one of Biology, Physics or Maths, and a strong record in them. She does not need A-levels.
  • A-levels (for comparison): A*AA, including at least an A in Chemistry and at least an A in one of Biology, Physics, Maths or Further Maths, all taken in the same year.
  • IB (for reference): 39 points, with 7, 6, 6 at Higher Level including Chemistry and one of Biology, Physics or Maths.
  • Age rule: you must be 18 by 1 November of the year you start. This is the rule behind the Transition Year warning in the roadmap.

Source: Oxford Medical Sciences Division, academic and age requirements, checked live in November 2026.

The test: UCAT (the BMAT is gone)

Older guides talk about a test called the BMAT. It was discontinued after the 2024 entry cycle, and Oxford has used the UCAT since 2025 entry. Any book or website that tells Maya to prepare for the BMAT is out of date.

Oxford publishes no fixed UCAT cut-off. It ranks applicants using the UCAT together with school grades. For 2026 entry, the average UCAT scores tell the story of how high the bar sits:

  • All applicants: 2,217.5 out of 2,700
  • Shortlisted for interview: 2,377.5
  • Offer holders: 2,407.1

Averages as reported by UKCAT People and Blue Peanut from Oxford Medical Sciences admissions statistics; treat them as a benchmark, not a threshold. Two questions the research could not settle from an official Oxford page: exactly how the Situational Judgement band is used, and how the UCAT is weighted for applicants like Maya who have no GCSEs (secondary guides say the UCAT counts double). Both are worth confirming with Oxford's admissions office when she applies.

The interview

If the UCAT and grades are strong enough, Oxford invites you to interview. Interviews happen online in December, and decisions arrive in January (12 January 2027 for 2027 entry). Oxford does not use the MMI circuit most schools use. Instead you get panel interviews, usually two or three of them, at two different colleges, each about 20 to 30 minutes.

The questions are mostly science problems to think through out loud: applied biology, chemistry and physiology, reading graphs and data, and reasoning about ethical dilemmas. They are not looking for rehearsed speeches about why you want to be a doctor. They want to watch how you think. Roughly a quarter to a third of applicants are interviewed, for around 165 places. There are no A100 places through Clearing.

What a college is

Oxford is not one single campus. It is a federation of more than 30 self-governing colleges. Every student belongs to one college: it admits you, houses you, looks after your welfare, and gives you weekly small-group teaching called tutorials, sometimes just you and one other student with an expert.

The University itself runs the lectures, labs and exams, and awards the degree. So Maya would apply to Oxford, live and learn day to day in her college, and graduate with an Oxford degree. Source: Oxford, college life.

The course itself: six years, two degrees

  1. Years 1 to 3, pre-clinical. First, how the body is built and how it works: anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, biochemistry and medical genetics, pathology, the nervous system, and the psychology of medicine, with visits to GP practices from early on. Then a deeper final stage with advanced topics, an essay, and a compulsory experimental research project of your own. At the end of Year 3 you earn a BA (Hons) in Medical Sciences.
  2. Years 4 to 6, clinical. Now you train in hospitals, mainly with Oxford University Hospitals NHS Trust doctors, and with local GPs. Year 4 runs 40 weeks; Years 5 and 6 run 48 weeks each, including a 10-week elective in Year 6, where students often go abroad. At the end you earn the BM BCh, the medical degree that lets you register provisionally with the GMC as a doctor, subject to passing the Medical Licensing Assessment.
  3. One modern wrinkle. Students are admitted to the pre-clinical stage first, then apply to move into Oxford's clinical stage in their final pre-clinical year. Since 2021, Oxford starters can no longer transfer to a London medical school for the clinical years.

Source: Oxford Medicine Course Information Sheet, 2026 entry (official PDF).

Money, and the scholarship question

The direct answer first: there is no Ireland-specific scholarship for Oxford, and no scholarship that pays for an Irish undergraduate to study medicine there. The famous names do not apply to Maya, and the reasons are worth knowing. But there is real help available, and this section separates what she can actually get from what she cannot.

The verdicts, award by award

Yes, she can get this

Oxford Bursary

Oxford's own bursary is explicitly open to UK students and Republic of Ireland nationals living in the UK or Ireland, on a first undergraduate degree, with household income of £50,000 or less. It is not repayable, and there is no separate application; it follows from the household income assessment. For 2026/27 it pays, per year: £4,390 (income up to £25,000), £3,850 (to £32,500), £3,290 (to £37,500), £2,190 (to £42,875) and £1,100 (to £50,000). The figures for 2027 entry are slightly higher. This is the main Oxford support Maya could actually receive.

Yes, she can get this

SUSI maintenance grant, taken to the UK

Ireland's SUSI grant can follow her to an approved full-time course in the UK, but only the maintenance part. The fee grant is not available outside Ireland. At 2026/27 Band 1 rates that is up to €4,722 a year (Oxford is well over 30 km from home, so the non-adjacent rate applies), or up to €7,936 on the special rate. It does not touch tuition, but tuition is covered by the loan anyway.

Yes, as a loan

UK tuition fee loan

Student Finance England will lend an Irish citizen the full tuition fee, £9,790 a year at 2026/27 rates, provided she has lived in the Common Travel Area for the three years before starting. It is repayable after graduation, and repayments depend on income. It is a loan, not a scholarship, but it means tuition never has to be found up front.

No, UK residents only

Crankstart Scholarship

Oxford's biggest undergraduate scholarship, worth £5,490 to £6,370 a year, is for students resident in the UK for at least three years before starting, not for education. Living in Ireland, Maya does not qualify. It would only come into play if the family had moved to the UK three or more years before she started. Do not count it.

No, twice over

Reach Oxford Scholarship

This one is often the first name people find, and it excludes Maya two ways. First, it is only for nationals of countries receiving OECD development assistance, and Ireland is not on that list. Second, it covers all subjects except medicine. Definitively not an option.

No, postgraduates only

Clarendon Fund and Rhodes Scholarship

Both are famous, both are fully funded, and both are for graduate study only. Clarendon supports outstanding graduate students at Oxford; the Rhodes requires a completed undergraduate degree (Ireland is a Rhodes constituency). Neither can fund a first degree in medicine. They only become relevant if Maya later goes back to Oxford for a research degree.

Maybe, small amounts

College bursaries and funds

Individual Oxford colleges add small top-ups of their own. For example, Jesus College's Access Bursaries pay £700 to £1,000 a year to UK and Irish undergraduates by household income, on top of the Oxford Bursary. Other colleges offer hardship funds and book, equipment and travel grants once you are there. Worth checking college by college at application time, but the amounts are hundreds, not thousands, and her college is decided during admissions, so none of it can be relied on in advance. No college was found offering a full scholarship for Irish medical students.

Uncertain, do not budget for it

NHS Bursary, years 5 and 6

From Year 5 of medicine in England, the NHS Bursary normally helps with tuition and living costs, but it is generally for students ordinarily resident in England. The NHS guide also describes a tuition-fee route for EU and EEA nationals living in the EU, which might cover Maya's tuition in Years 5 and 6, but whether an Irish citizen living in Ireland qualifies in 2035 could not be verified. The NHS itself warns students not to rely on current funding when planning future years. Treat this as a possible bonus, never as part of the plan.

The one long shot

Ellison Undergraduate Scholars Programme

Run by the Ellison Institute of Technology (a separate organisation from Oxford University), this is the only scheme found that could fully fund her: it is open to all nationalities and all Oxford undergraduate subjects including Medicine A100. Secondary sources describe it as fully funded, fees and living costs, but that package was not verified on the Institute's own pages during this research, and the cohort is tiny and extremely competitive. Applications come first, well before UCAS (the deadline for October 2027 entry was 31 July 2026). A lottery ticket, not a plan.

None found

Irish government or charity funding for Oxford medicine

No Irish government scheme and no Irish charity was found that funds undergraduate medicine at Oxford, or in the UK generally, beyond SUSI maintenance. (The well-known Mitchell Scholarship funds postgraduate study in Ireland for Americans, which is the opposite direction.) A small local or community fund could exist without appearing in searches, so it cannot be ruled out absolutely, but nothing national exists in the sources checked.

Sources: Oxford, bursaries and scholarships; Oxford, Reach Oxford Scholarship; Oxford Finance Guide 2026/27; Ellison Institute of Technology, Scholars FAQs; NHS Business Services Authority, NHS Bursary.

What a year at Oxford actually costs an Irish student

Item (2026/27 prices, years 1 to 3)Amount
Tuition fee, Home rate (Ireland pays Home, not the £49,400 overseas rate)£9,790 / yr
Tuition fee loan from Student Finance Englandcovers it in full, repayable later
Living costs, Oxford's own estimate, 9 months (£1,405 to £2,105 a month: rent £825 to £990, food £315 to £545, the rest personal, social and study costs)£12,645 to £18,945 / yr
Oxford Bursary, if household income is £25,000 or lessminus up to £4,390 / yr
SUSI maintenance, Band 1 non-adjacent, if the family qualifiesminus up to €4,722 / yr
Cash the family still has to find, best case (converting the SUSI euro at roughly £0.87, for illustration only)about £4,200 to £10,500 / yr
Cash to find with no bursary and no SUSI (household income above both limits), plus travel home, books and equipment£12,645 to £18,945 / yr

The clinical years cost more. They are longer than the 9-month pre-clinical years: Year 4 runs 40 weeks and Years 5 and 6 run 48 weeks each, so budget roughly 11 months of living costs a year across the clinical years, about £15,500 to £23,000 at the same monthly rates. Oxford suggests allowing about 4% a year for cost increases.

Six-year totals, at today's prices held flat: about £58,700 of tuition borrowed (less, if the NHS Bursary ever covers Years 5 and 6), and £84,000 to £126,000 of living costs across the six years, reduced in the best case by about £26,300 of Oxford Bursary plus €28,300 of SUSI maintenance. Compare Ireland: tuition free, no tuition debt at all, and the cash cost is the student contribution (often SUSI-covered) plus living costs. Oxford is possible, and the loan means tuition is never the blocker, but the family should expect to fund several thousand pounds a year of living costs for six years. No scholarship makes it free.

Sources: Oxford Medicine Course Information Sheet 2026; Oxford Finance Guide 2025/26. Oxford's Home fee is set to rise to £10,050 in 2027/28.

For grown-ups: the checklist and the open questions

The decision points, in order

  • Secondary school choice (2029): check whether the school offers Transition Year, and whether it is optional or compulsory there. This quietly decides the Oxford age question.
  • Start of 5th year: Higher Chemistry and Higher Biology (plus Higher Maths if manageable). This is the single most consequential choice on the whole road.
  • 6th year, autumn: if the UK is in play, the UCAS deadline is 15 October, months before the CAO closes on 1 February. The UCAT is sat the summer before. The two application systems run in parallel and both can be used.
  • 6th year, February: HPAT for Ireland, registered separately with ACER. Score valid for that year only.
  • Money: SUSI is assessed on the prior calendar year's household income and applies to UK study for maintenance only. The Oxford Bursary follows from the Student Finance England income assessment. Neither needs a separate scholarship application.
  • Fee status: the Home-fee advantage depends on Maya being an Irish citizen and resident in Ireland or the Common Travel Area for the three years before the course starts. Worth protecting.

Honest open questions

  • NHS Bursary in Years 5 and 6: unverified for an Irish citizen living in Ireland. Confirm with NHSBSA and Student Finance in the application year; do not budget for it.
  • How Oxford weights the UCAT without GCSEs, and whether the Situational Judgement band is used in shortlisting: not confirmed on an official Oxford page. Ask the Medical Sciences admissions office nearer the time.
  • Ellison Scholars funding: eligibility for medicine is confirmed on the Institute's own FAQ, but the "fully funded" package comes from secondary sources. Check eit.org directly if she ever applies.
  • Irish universities and starting at 17: no age-18 rule was found for Irish medical schools (unlike Oxford's), but it was not explicitly confirmed with any university either.
  • Everything will move: the HPAT is already being reweighted from 2027, and fee caps, SUSI thresholds, NHS funding and even the Common Travel Area arrangements could change before 2034. The structure is stable; the numbers are not. Re-check everything in 5th and 6th year.

And finally, for Maya. Doctors are not made in one big jump. They are made of thousands of small steps: a book finished, a hard sum worked out, a kind word to someone who is sad, a question asked in science class. You are already walking the road. Keep going, enjoy the walk, and we will check the map together again when the turns get closer.
